name: Rich Brennan
one_paragraph: Brennan is an Australia-based systematic trend follower who calls himself an 'outlier hunter'. He treats markets as complex adaptive, reflexive, path-dependent and non-ergodic feedback systems: price moves because orders have impact (not because news reveals value), trends are the reinforcing structure left when divergent (trend, momentum, stop-loss, passive buy-the-biggest) participants outweigh convergent (value, mean-reversion, market-maker) ones, and a few rare outlier trends (cocoa, gold, wheat, coffee) make nearly all the profit while 60-70% of trades lose. He therefore does not predict: he keeps the widest feasible, mostly absolute-momentum, medium-to-long-horizon universe (just under 100 markets) as a watch list, enters small ATR-normalised equal-risk bets, runs an ensemble of structurally different trend systems with trailing stops that switch on one after another as a trend persists, sizes new risk from closed (realised) balance rather than open equity, and never cuts a winner because volatility rose. He rejects Gaussian tools (Sharpe, VaR, Kelly, expectancy, vol targeting) because calm stores hidden fragility and survival, not average return, is the test; he wants convexity (small linear losses, open right tail), walk-forward testing on untouched data, loosely parameterised plateau rules, and a long live record. His market views follow one regime story: coordinated central banks and QE (roughly 2010-2018) compressed trends, whereas a fragmented, decoupled, multipolar world after 2020 (stated most strongly 2026-01) is the best environment for trend following in years. His evidence is mostly first principles, analogy (weather, avalanche, race car) and his own unpublished simulations/tests (68-market Hurst/kurtosis fingerprint, agent-based model with a 20-30% divergent threshold, 68-market subset test) described verbally without figures.

core_beliefs.belief: Trend-following profit comes from rare outlier moves in the fat tails (a few trades make the whole curve); the bulk of the return distribution is noise or mean-reverting, the location of the next outlier is unknowable, so he diversifies widely to catch it rather than to reduce risk.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - same logic from 2024-10 (watch list) to 2026-07 (cocoa, fractal right tails); only the number of markets varies by account size (about 10 at $200k up to just under 100 for his own book)

core_beliefs.belief: Markets are complex adaptive systems; trends, fat tails and volatility clustering are generated by feedback among participants (divergent/reinforcing versus convergent/balancing), not by news or fair value, so trend following harvests a structural feature rather than a temporary inefficiency. Calm = balancing dominates, ranging; trends = reinforcing dominates; phase transition between.
core_beliefs.stable: stable in substance, evolved in rigour: 2024 version is analogy (Holland, West, ants, coastlines); 2026 version cites his own tests (Hurst 0.62-0.82 rolling, 0.866 full sample, tail exponent 3.33, vol clustering 0.353, 68 markets) and an agent model whose divergent threshold is quoted as 20-25% (MT017), 25-30% (MT222), about 25% (MT224)

core_beliefs.belief: Price moves because of trade impact (supply and demand pressure, square-root law), not because information is revealed; news is a trigger, the market's internal state sets the size; fundamentals, macro and flows are downstream; about 90% of big moves are endogenous.
core_beliefs.stable: stable; the cocoa 2024 case shows the mix he allows (exogenous Africa supply news started it, endogenous flows accelerated it: MT019-C13-4)

core_beliefs.belief: Trends and mean reversion come from collective trader impact, not human behavioural bias (prospect theory is a symptom), so AI agents will not remove them; AI will compress short-term prediction horizons and thereby favour structure-based trend following.
core_beliefs.stable: stable (2024-06 to 2025-11); MT057 is hedged ('quietly confident', doubts forecasting skill at long horizons)

core_beliefs.belief: Gaussian/backward-looking risk tools (Sharpe, standard deviation, VaR, Kelly, expectancy, fixed volatility targeting) misstate risk. Risk is vulnerability/the unforeseen, not historical variance; five-sigma events occur far more often than normal models imply (32 in 30 years of ES futures; 5,791x as frequent).
core_beliefs.stable: stable; the object of attack widens over time (2024-12 VaR/Sharpe; 2025-10 Kelly and expectancy; 2026-03 fixed vol targeting; 2026-07 Sharpe as construction-blind). MT222 admits the research offers no replacement

core_beliefs.belief: Calm is not safe: low volatility is stored, compressed risk (leverage, concentration, price-insensitive positioning accumulate) that a small trigger releases; volatility clusters, so calm persists until the transition catches everyone. Insurance (options) is cheapest when most valuable.
core_beliefs.stable: stable; by 2026 he ties it to specific mechanisms (vol-targeted models raising size in calm, structured products, passive)

core_beliefs.belief: Convexity is the goal: small linear losses (small bets, stops), open uncapped gains (anti-martingale, ensemble), a barbell; trend following is convexity for opportunity capture with no explicit premium (the implicit premium is whipsaw, foregone growth, gap risk). Options are the more precise hedge. Positive skew maximises compounded wealth.
core_beliefs.stable: stable; MT224 adds that trend plus long options is 'both worlds' and calls long-vol overlays on traditional portfolios a band-aid

core_beliefs.belief: Wealth is multiplicative and path dependent (non-ergodic, floor at zero), so order of returns and ruin matter more than expectancy; survival is the true measure of success for systems and managers.

Backtests always overfit and cannot predict returns; use them for stress and sensitivity tests, and take benchmarks only from a walk-forward run on untouched out-of-sample data (realistic drawdown 35-40% versus 5-10% in backtest). Prefer many models, loose plateau parameters (50 vs 200 days, not 47), ensembles over lookbacks; tight optimisation is an emotional comfort betting on stationarity.
core_beliefs.stable: stable; but he himself reports backtest-type results (68-market subset test, 10 vs 20 model test, 40-year reshuffles) - see internal_tensions

core_beliefs.belief: 'Trend follower' covers several species with different objectives (replicators, core diversifiers, crisis-risk-offset, outlier hunters; earlier: idiosyncratic versus correlation-conscious tribes). Design choices (breadth, absolute versus cross-sectional momentum, vol targeting, symmetry, speed) follow from the objective, so most debates and league-table metrics talk past each other; dispersion is healthy if managers state objectives.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved: 2025-06 two tribes (idiosyncratic vs correlation-conscious), 2025-08 four species; the underlying point (objective dictates design) unchanged

core_beliefs.belief: A long validated live track record is the only universal metric; stay with a stable process through bad stretches, do not change models after pain, judge on the next 2,000-4,000 trades not the last 1-3 years, and explain underperformance against the stated objective.
Medium-to-long-term trend following is more robust than shorter horizons (short horizons are more mean reverting and the AI-competitive space; fast systems get whipsawed out of long trends).
core_beliefs.stable: stable; evidence cited as 'all the data I have seen' (MT019) and design reasoning, not shown

core_beliefs.belief: Policy regime sets the trend environment: coordinated central banks/QE and buy-the-dip compressed and truncated trends (2010-2018 'the anomaly'); post-2020 decoupling, deglobalisation and fragmentation let regional imbalances persist, favouring idiosyncratic single-market trends; frequent policy whipsaw is the main risk to this view.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved in strength: 2024-12 'decoupling producing outlier trends'; 2025-06 idiosyncratic tribe favoured; 2025-10 'trend heaven' unless whipsaw; 2026-01 'best period in years'; 2026-03 tail-event regime favours trend and long vol. Not tested with data in any appearance

core_beliefs.belief: Diversification should be by structurally uncorrelated systems and trade-return correlation (butterfly effect: Brent vs WTI price correlation high but ensemble trade returns quite uncorrelated), not by price correlation, which is fickle; but diversification is not a cure for correlation (permanent coupling) and mainly adds exposure to right-tail events.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved/partly contradicted on how many systems: about 20 (MT006, 2024-10), 10 versus 20 depends on regime (MT063, 2024-12), 5 for retail and ~10 saturation (MT181, MT166, 2025) - no reason given for the revision

core_beliefs.belief: Hold position size static after entry (equal ATR-normalised small bets); vol targeting cuts the largest winners just as a trend accelerates, so breadth, not vol targeting, is the outlier hunter's risk control. Size from closed balance, cap leverage, equal-risk rather than Kelly or edge-tilted sizing.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved: 2024-06 fixed-dollar risk per trade with 25-day ATR stop (MT057); 2025-02 risk a small fraction of closed core capital; 2025-08 static small bets; 2025-10 closed-balance sizing; 2026-07 absolute leverage cap and equal risk. No reason given for each step beyond the convexity/path-dependence logic

core_beliefs.belief: The future is unfinished and reflexive, so path prediction is futile; trend following recognises existing structure (persistence, volatility clustering) and responds. Macro forecasts are hypotheses to be confirmed by the market before acting.
core_beliefs.stable: stable in 2025-2026; compare internal_tensions (earlier 'mostly predictable regime' language)

core_beliefs.belief: Rule-based, pre-committed systems beat discretion because humans are emotional under pressure; psychology (overriding rules) is the weak point of trend followers; strong emotions are a design signal to reduce size.

Passive growth (about 60% of US equity fund assets) shifts ownership from price-sensitive to price-insensitive, diluting balancing agents, thinning the float and raising price impact per dollar (multiplier about 5, range 3-7), which hardens the trend engine; structured products/vol-suppression may hurt trend and build fragility.
core_beliefs.stable: stable; he concedes the multiplier needs verification (MT017-C15-X1)

mechanisms.name: Divergent versus convergent feedback creates trends, fat tails and clustering (agent-based model)
chain: random traders only -> Gaussian returns, no memory
add convergent (value, mean-reversion, market-maker) traders -> still Gaussian, oscillation around equilibrium
divergent (trend, momentum, stop-loss, margin call, passive buy-the-biggest) share crosses about 20-30% -> abrupt phase transition: fat tails, vol clustering, Hurst above 0.85

no news input needed -> same signatures as 68 real futures markets (Hurst 0.62-0.82 rolling; 0.866, tail exponent 3.33, vol autocorrelation 0.353 since 1984) -> trend following is a structural harvest
mechanisms.fails_when: Not stated; threshold is model-specific, no real-market measurement of divergent share given; sufficiency, not necessity; quiet range regimes are below threshold but are not evidence of failure

mechanisms.name: Reinforcing cascade: spark versus dry wood
chain: small breakout or imbalance -> momentum systems buy
realised volatility changes -> vol-targeting and rebalancing adjust across portfolios
position shifts force further price adjustment -> cascade larger than trigger
balancing feedback (market makers, value, risk managers) -> temporary calm; without it loops grow to collapse; exhaustion -> fast violent reversal and renewal
mechanisms.fails_when: When balancing dominates the market ranges rather than trends; timing of exhaustion not predictable

mechanisms.name: Trader impact across scales
chain: each order shifts supply/demand for the next (square-root impact)
small aligned trades compound; vol clusters
short-horizon zigzags cancel (mean reversion) while reinforcing impacts add up as scale lengthens
coherence across scales -> serial correlation = trend
mechanisms.fails_when: When positive feedback is exhausted (valuation stretch, concentration)

mechanisms.name: Passive dilution and inelastic markets
chain: rising price-insensitive share (passive, benchmark-huggers) -> price-sensitive agents shrink as a share
less capital pushes back on price in motion -> overshoots and cascades
thin price-sensitive float -> $1 of net flow moves market cap about $5 (range 3-7)
bigger directional moves per dollar -> more favourable trend environment
mechanisms.fails_when: Retirees drawing down passive holdings may reverse growth; concentration could end in an extinction-level unwind; multiplier from a small set of studies; threshold crossed long ago so not visible in fingerprint

mechanisms.name: Calm builds fragility, a small shock releases it
chain: calm regime / low realised vol (vol clusters) -> vol-targeted models mechanically raise size; participants lever up to earn a living; correlations tighten
hidden leverage, concentration, feedback loops accumulate; Sharpe/VaR on history show little risk; options cheap
coupling oscillation cancels in calm; a small perturbation -> explosion, then coupling turns to trend and everything correlates
capital destruction comes mainly from quiet markets with oversized positions

mechanisms.name: Ensemble of uncorrelated systems with staggered activation and trailing stops (outlier hunting)
chain: wide watch list, small bets, capital mostly inactive in noise
uncorrelated entry systems (Donchian, Keltner, Bollinger and others) activate at different times; more models invested as trend matures -> concentrates on winners by rule
trailing stop on every system -> many tight stops aggregate to a looser overall exit; open profit not given back
one outlier pays for dozens of small losses ('infinite yield'); in outlier-free periods extra models add whipsaw (30-40% win rate)
mechanisms.fails_when: Margin limits cap about 20 systems; no outliers or predictable regime: 10 beat 20 models; trend dissipates early -> only a few activated systems lose; correlated markets reversing together (Oct 2024)

mechanisms.name: Trade correlation versus price correlation (butterfly effect)
chain: outlier has a nonlinear volatile path -> single model is snagged by volatility and misses it
tiny differences in initial price paths -> widely dispersed trade results
same ensemble on Brent and WTI -> quite uncorrelated return streams despite highly correlated prices
so highly price-correlated markets can both be traded by an outlier hunter
mechanisms.fails_when: Not stated; claim restricted to outlier-hunter ensembles, conventional wisdom holds for nearly all other models

mechanisms.name: Breadth as lottery tickets (68-market subset test)
chain: few trades produce most profit; location of next outlier unknowable
hold widest feasible liquid universe; accept many unprofitable markets (27 of 68 lost money, book MAR 0.8) and dead spells (cocoa about 15 years)
cut to random 30 of 68 -> 88% chance of underperforming full book on MAR; only 35 of 300 subsets (12%) exceed MAR 0.8
new capital goes to new liquid markets first, not larger bets or more systems
mechanisms.fails_when: Liquidity, counterparty or regulatory risk limits breadth; for core diversifiers or crisis-offset managers breadth can dilute; single test of 2020-01-01 to 2025-07-31 dominated by wheat and cocoa, not out-of-sample

mechanisms.name: Static small bets versus volatility targeting
chain: volatility spikes mid-trend (crude vol doubles in a big uptrend) -> a vol targeter cuts exactly as trend accelerates and clips the biggest winner
equal small ATR-normalised bets left unchanged -> each loss small, each winner runs; breadth keeps each bet small
fixed vol target also sized to recent calm vol -> positions fit to the centre of a fat-tailed distribution
mechanisms.fails_when: Mandate with vol budget and low drawdown tolerance (smoothing suits replicators and core diversifiers); host: static positions can balloon (vol 35 to 95) and vol targeting can raise risk after quiet spells; Dunn uses daily risk target, not vol target

mechanisms.name: Path dependence and closed-balance sizing
chain: non-ergodic, multiplicative wealth with floor at zero -> order of wins/losses decides outcome; -50% then +50% leaves a permanent hole
Sharpe, Sortino, VaR, std dev are invariant to reshuffling the same 40 years yet terminal wealth ranged from a 30% to an 84% decline
size new positions from closed (realised) balance -> exposure falls automatically in drawdowns, scales up only after confirmed gains
large size on 5% positive expectancy -> drag and ruin; very small size on a 2% expectancy system (30% win, 3:1 payoff) compounds
mechanisms.fails_when: Host: inflows and inception date break the logic for funds; open equity in liquid futures is not illusory; Kelly-style sizing works only if assumptions hold (LTCM did well while they held)

mechanisms.name: Kelly and edge-tilted sizing lose to equal risk
chain: Kelly optimum is a peak needing perfect information -> any overshoot goes to ruin through vol drag
fat tails and non-stationarity make the required sample explode; noise often exceeds signal
ranking markets by apparent edge and tilting size rebuilds a single cable and misses explosions such as cocoa
equal-risk, fractional sizing and widening the book instead

mechanisms.name: Convexity and barbell: brakes allow speed
chain: limit adverse volatility with brakes defined in advance (stops, small size); do not limit beneficial volatility
extreme months dominate compounding (10 best S&P months about 30% of growth, 10 worst about 40% drag over 40 years)
barbell: minimise adverse exposure, stay open to unlimited upside; permanently conservative sizing removes upside too
trend following embeds this via stops, anti-martingale adding and wide diversification; martingale is the concave opposite
mechanisms.fails_when: Short-term shocks hit medium-to-long models before positions change; whipsaw; reported decline in trend skew (host)

mechanisms.name: Policy regime to trend environment
chain: post-GFC QE and coordinated central banks, stable inflation -> compression, buy-the-dip, truncated trends (2010-2018 anomaly); correlation-conscious cross-sectional, vol-targeted managers win 2008-2020
stored energy released from 2020 -> strong trends
globalisation reverses; regional imbalances (energy, inflation, currency, trade) persist with slow release valves -> idiosyncratic single-market trends (cocoa, soybeans, gold)
risk: policy whipsaw (first six months of 2025, April tariffs) and political shocks produce chop
mechanisms.fails_when: Frequent policy changes create whipsaw ('death by a thousand cuts'); counterparty per host: big managers' drawdowns also from financial-futures tilt

mechanisms.name: Why backtests mislead; walk-forward fix
chain: full history in hindsight -> selection among parameter streams and fit to the known event order
overfit backtest -> upward-biased expectation and drawdown 5-10%
develop on 1970-2000 only, run frozen once on 2000-2024 -> realistic drawdown 35-40%, CAGR, volatility
touching out-of-sample data to select models -> contamination
mechanisms.fails_when: Out-of-sample data reused; trend followers cannot expect no OOS decay (regime dependence), unlike mean-reversion modellers

mechanisms.name: Analytically optimal trend rules (Markov / semi-Markov) as support, not edge
chain: serial correlation across lags = autoregression = Markov model
plain Markov -> EMA best; semi-Markov (trend ending likelier with age) -> MACD best, with practitioner-like medium-long loose parameters
convergence with brute-force backtests -> rules are not data-mined; trend models as thermometers of hidden state; regime forecasts reliable only days to a week
mechanisms.fails_when: Not a holy grail; forecast skill confined to short term; paper equity-derived, ported to futures by Stark (Sharpe about 1.2)

mechanisms.name: Objective determines design (four species)
chain: objective (track index, diversify, offset crises, harvest outliers) -> archetype with its own market count, momentum type, sizing, speed
archetype -> matching metric (tracking error; portfolio Sharpe/correlation; crisis-period CAGR; skew and top-trade share)
wrong metric or borrowed rules -> style drift and weaker survivability
mechanisms.fails_when: Mixed objectives; host says a fifth 'pure trend' archetype exists and must be proven

mechanisms.name: Absolute versus cross-sectional momentum; asymmetric rules; speed
chain: cross-sectional ranking trims weak markets, tilts to leaders -> smoother, suits replicators/core diversifiers
same ranking for an outlier hunter -> sells into strength and cuts lifetime winners; use pure absolute momentum
asymmetry reflects structure: commodity spikes are supply-shock longs, equity collapses violent on short side -> wider room for commodity longs, wider trailing stops on equity shorts
slow systems sit through volatility to catch multi-month moves; fast ones whipsawed
mechanisms.fails_when: Host: asymmetric rules may be optimisation, identical rules arguably more robust; crisis-offset objectives may justify short speeds (host: 2025 short-term funds did not deliver)

mechanisms.name: Oil spike as a coiled market (March 2026)
chain: 18 months of drift lower, heavy shorts, suppressed vol, amplifiers gone -> structurally coiled
geopolitical catalyst -> outsized spike 66 to 119 as divergent share crosses threshold
spike-chasers stopped out -> 30% reversal to 84 in days; if disruption sustained -> genuine trend, otherwise mid-70s
sustained oil -> cost pass-through, fast central-bank hikes, high-inflation high-rates regime (1990s analogy), big CTA trends
mechanisms.fails_when: Disruption resolved or never sustained; single episode

mechanisms.name: Bad futures data contaminates backtests; LLM-generated strategies overfit
chain: contract rolls leave artificial gaps -> Panama back-adjustment shifts all earlier levels (can go negative) -> rules with absolute price thresholds, long-lookback percent returns, mean reversion to long averages or fixed dollar stops mislead
roll logic, survivorship, granularity mismatch -> backtest/live divergence
LLMs pattern-match popular indicator stacks -> mass-mined false positives, hindsight bias; embed causal logic in the prompt, use LLMs for debugging
mechanisms.fails_when: Engines rejecting negative prices need another adjustment

playbook.rule: Systematic, non-predictive trend following, pure absolute (time-series) momentum, no cross-sectional overlay, no judgement about fair value or news; medium-to-long horizon; recognise structural trends (serial-correlation outliers), not visual patterns.
playbook.why: Harvests the structural feedback engine; ranking sells strength and cuts lifetime winners; short horizons are mean-reverting and AI-contested.

playbook.rule: Ensemble of about 8 structurally different entry systems (Donchian, Keltner, Bollinger breakouts, volatility expansion, smooth persistence, mean-reversion-into-trend) with parameter variations, 10 to 20 per market depending on outlier regime; combine several lookbacks instead of choosing one.
playbook.why: Single system is snagged by outlier volatility; ensemble reduces hindsight parameter reliance; no lookback is best year to year (2025: 20-day worst, 60-day slightly positive, 130/260 negative).

playbook.rule: Optionally asymmetric: more room (looser exits) for commodity longs and wider trailing stops on equity shorts; crisis-offset managers favour bond/safe-haven longs.
playbook.why: Commodity spikes are supply-shock rallies, equity crashes fall violently, commodities near lows have limited downside tail.

playbook.rule: Treat macro forecasts as hypotheses and act only when price confirms (e.g. short bonds only if bonds actually sell off); do not pre-decide whether a spike is repricing or overshoot.
playbook.why: The market is the final arbiter; future price path is not yet built.

playbook.rule: Widest feasible liquid and semi-liquid universe, just under 100 markets (outlier-hunter archetype 100+; his earlier tests 68 markets, a 60-70 market ensemble for retail), including small ones (live cattle, rubber, milk, cocoa); avoid off-exchange or weakly regulated markets.
playbook.why: A few trades make the curve; missing the parabolic market costs more than a messy book; liquidity/counterparty/regulatory risk is the cap.

playbook.rule: Retail scaling: about $200k = about 10 uncorrelated markets with 5 ensemble systems; about 30 markets at $400k; about 60 at $1M; micro/nano futures and standard contracts; extend short micro histories with a proxy standard contract.
playbook.why: Small capital cannot size equal risk across 100 markets; over-diversified $10k accounts take hidden correlation and ruin.

playbook.rule: Treat the universe as a watch list: small allocation when an outlier emerges, add as it endures; do not hold positions in everything.
playbook.why: Diversification gives coverage without forcing participation in noise.

playbook.rule: Equal small ATR-normalised risk at entry per market (earlier: fixed dollar risk per trade, e.g. $500, stop at a multiple of 25-day ATR, contracts = risk / stop distance); do not resize down for later volatility rises; add via ensemble (anti-martingale), never double after losses.
playbook.why: Preserves convexity; breadth keeps each bet small; vol targeting clips winners.

playbook.rule: Size new positions from closed (realised) balance, not floating equity; keep individual sizes small even with positive expectancy; cap leverage in absolute terms; equal-risk fractional sizing rather than tilting to apparent edge. Allocate new outside AUM on closed equity.
playbook.why: Auto-reduces exposure in drawdown, scales only after confirmed gains; non-ergodic ruin; edge differences below estimation noise.

playbook.rule: As trend persists, more systems activate, concentrating risk in winners by rule; start small when signals suggest a possible outlier and add as it succeeds.
playbook.why: Avoid committing all capital before the trend is an outlier.

playbook.rule: Trailing stop on every system at all times; small bet size as the ultimate stop (stops can gap); stops, position limits and drawdown rules defined before the trade; accept an exit only if a pre-written rule triggered it.
playbook.why: Cannot give back open profit as an outlier turns; brakes are commitments, otherwise exits are rationalised emotion.

playbook.rule: Do not use volatility, VaR, Sharpe or other statistical measures to protect the portfolio; protect through non-overfit design, sizing, convexity and a barbell; judge a portfolio by architecture and hidden single dependencies (does it have one failure mode or many).
playbook.why: Gaussian assumptions fail; Sharpe ignores construction; diversification across a common anchor is one bet.

playbook.rule: Use correlation as a between-instrument diagnostic of how shocks travel and variance (ATR) as the within-instrument control that shrinks size when variance rises; add position-level drawdown management.
playbook.why: Correlation tells the weather, variance whether to put on another coat (stated 2026-05).

playbook.rule: Grow by adding new liquid markets first, not larger bets; stop adding systems at about 10 (earlier: up to about 20 until margin binds); diversify systems by behaviour not by correlation; consider combining trend with explicit long-option protection and pairing equities with trend or long vol.
playbook.why: Unknown location of next outlier; 50/50 S&P and trend yields near sum of returns because correlation turns negative in crises.

playbook.rule: Develop on in-sample data only (e.g. 1970-2000, multi-market over 30 years, about 100 markets); run frozen models once on out-of-sample (2000-2024); compare backtest, OOS and adaptive walk-forward curves and set drawdown/CAGR/vol expectations from the OOS curve; backtest only for sensitivity/stress, never for expected return.
playbook.why: Backtest always best and unrealistic; touched OOS data is tainted.

playbook.rule: Prefer plateau parameters (50 vs 200 days, not 47) and a large ensemble to few optimised systems; test mechanisms with minimal agent-based models and Hurst/kurtosis fingerprints in rolling 5-year windows; test breadth by random blind subsets against the full-book MAR distribution; evaluate wealth path-dependently (reshuffle returns, include cash flows).
playbook.why: Less overfitting; standard statistics hide survival risk and order effects.

playbook.rule: Build own back-adjusted continuous futures series (Panama) with one consistent roll trigger identical to live; include delisted contracts; use adjustment-agnostic indicators (avoid absolute price thresholds, long-lookback percent returns, mean reversion to long averages, fixed dollar stops); use LLMs only for debugging and code porting.
playbook.why: Backtest/live divergence and survivorship; LLMs pattern-match and cannot judge causal soundness.

playbook.rule: Judge systems and managers by survival and a long validated live record (the next 2,000 trades), keep a stable process through bad stretches, do not change models after drawdowns.
playbook.why: Only universal metric; behavioural drift (Winton example) erodes survivability.

playbook.rule: Predetermined entries and exits, automation, and size that keeps losses tolerable; control only entry, exit, size and adherence; strong emotion = redesign (reduce size).
playbook.why: Humans decide poorly under pressure.

playbook.rule: Re-import actual broker costs (spread, slippage, swap/financing) after the first backtest and drop markets/models that become untradeable; monitor CFD swap on a dashboard (positive swap adds carry to trend); check per-contract fees on nanos.
playbook.why: Costs and financing can eliminate marginal markets or long-hold performance.

playbook.rule: Allocator view: classify CTA peers into archetypes, decide which the portfolio needs, pick the best one or two in each, judging each on its own metric; present own objective and expected performance and explain underperformance against it. Faber-style long-only 10-month overlay is risk mitigation, not a hedge; options for short-term protection.
playbook.why: No single manager delivers all objectives; objectives differ.

evidence_style: Mostly first principles and analogy from complex-systems science (Holland, West, Wolfram, Mandelbrot, Bouchaud, Peters, Gabaix; weather ensembles, avalanche, sandpile, race car, F1, starlings) plus Dredge/Taleb convexity ideas, backed by his own research that is reported verbally and not shown: walk-forward vs backtest comparison, 10 vs 20 model test, 68-market Hurst/kurtosis fingerprint, agent-based model, 40-year reshuffles, 125-year Dow/S&P fractal analysis, 68-market random-subset test. Anecdotes (cocoa, wheat 2022, oil 2026, Brisbane floods, LTCM, Winton). Several numbers are cited without source (40-year S&P months, 60% passive, WHO fertility, 5,791x). Very little displayed data; several claims explicitly unpublished. Some qualification under challenge (multiplier needs verification; markets may not be exactly fractal; holds 'quietly confident' on AI).

views_timeline.view: Trend models are in a choppy whipsaw period; AI will quickly dominate short-term prediction but not medium-to-long-term trend following.
views_timeline.reasoning: Mixed success across assets; uncertainty compounds with horizon, Renaissance external fund marginal at long horizons.

views_timeline.view: Early-August 2024 shock was short and reversed; losses came from Nikkei, yen and equity indexes; commodities kept trending; AI will not end trends or mean reversion.
views_timeline.reasoning: AI agents are traders whose orders exert impact; monthly statistics hide intra-month volatility.

views_timeline.view: October 2024 very difficult for his systems: energy reversed, coffee hurt, everything reversed at once despite diversification; dispersion a major 2024 theme. Faber-style long-only overlay on SPY/TLT/EEM is valid but slow and whipsaw-prone.
views_timeline.reasoning: Hidden correlations across a large market matrix; slow exits, sacrificed upside.

views_timeline.view: Outliers (Bitcoin, gold, Australian dollar, coffee, orange juice) drove 2024 trend returns yet dispersion was large; would rather trade his trend models than chase equity returns; geopolitics escalating (ruble, Kursk).
views_timeline.reasoning: Long-term performance across regimes is the best measure; sanctions as complex-system interplay.

views_timeline.view: Decoupling in financial markets is producing outlier trends in smaller markets (cocoa, coffee, OJ, bitcoin, yen crosses); not a big fan of CTA replication yet.
views_timeline.reasoning: Moves in smaller markets; replication lacks a track record across regimes.

views_timeline.view: Good January for his firm driven by commodities such as coffee while SG Trend Index fell; markets non-linear and risk comes from the unforeseen; convexity matters most now.
views_timeline.reasoning: Different exposures and model designs; long muted regimes then explosive moves; 60/40 correlation shift.

views_timeline.view: Trend followers are deep in drawdown (April cruel, SG Trend Index at its worst monthly drawdown); the whipsaw regime should not last because a direction must emerge; idiosyncratic single-market trends are favoured post-2020; retail trend following viable from about $200k.
views_timeline.reasoning: Tariffs hit all sectors at once; lost central-bank coordination and fragmentation; micro/nano futures.

views_timeline.view: Trends emerged mid-2025 after a very hard first half (equities, metals, meats, Bitcoin paying, copper reversal hurt); hopes book recovers to roughly break-even for the year.
views_timeline.reasoning: Observation of his book's P&L by sector.

views_timeline.view: Bullish on trend following after a difficult first six months of 2025 (policy whipsaw): 'trend heaven' with decoupled, less coordinated central banks; trend models turning long in energies, metals may breathe; buy-the-dip expected to fade; AI shortens prediction horizons; precious-metals reversal is feedback inverting.
views_timeline.reasoning: Policy whipsaw faded; post-GFC to 2018 was the anomaly; positive feedback exhausted after long rise.

views_timeline.view: Dispersion in trend following is healthy; managers are a broad church and must explain objectives.
views_timeline.reasoning: Different designs (outlier hunters, benchmark chasers, crisis alpha); design decisions never obvious.

views_timeline.view: Fragmented, multipolar world is the best period for trend following in years; 2025 was a metals-led concentration year (metals about 21%), April the worst drawdown; gold trend intact, platinum a late leader.
views_timeline.reasoning: Persistent regional imbalances without coordinated central-bank intervention; metals recovered the drawdown while currencies, bonds and energy lost.

views_timeline.view: Oil spike (66 to 119 to 84) is a coiled-spring overshoot: resolved disruption means mid-70s, sustained means a genuine trend and a high-inflation, high-rate regime good for trend followers; regime ahead (tail events in metals, energy, deglobalisation) favours trend and long vol and hurts pod shops; markets will not revert to the old normal.
views_timeline.reasoning: Participant-mix threshold; 1990s analogy; most strategies fail in tail regimes.

views_timeline.view: Passive growth is hardening the trend engine (thinner float, higher multiplier) so trend opportunity is increasing; S&P rising while the world around it falls; structured-product vol suppression may hurt trend and build fragility; passive concentration could end in an extinction-level unwind; Trend Barometer at 39% shows trend weakness.
views_timeline.reasoning: Passive dilutes balancing agents and leaves reinforcing ones intact; calm regimes lose strategy diversity.

views_timeline.view: Trend followers had a volatile, challenging couple of months with a significant cocoa decline after it was the big winner; cocoa-type explosive idiosyncratic winners justify maximal diversification and equal-risk sizing.
views_timeline.reasoning: One-line status; repeated cocoa example for breadth.

how_views_changed: The framework is constant from 2024-06 to 2026-07 (complex adaptive systems, outliers, ensemble, convexity, distrust of Gaussian tools). What changes: (1) Rigour of the claims: 2024 reasoning is analogy and Faber/Holland-style theory; 2026 episodes cite his own quantified research (Hurst 0.866, tail exponent 3.33, 68 markets since 1984, agent-model threshold, 40-year reshuffles). He gives no explicit reason for this shift (the research phases are mentioned as his own factors-of-finance work). (2) Sizing: 2024-06 fixed-dollar risk with 25-day ATR stop; 2024-12 vol targeting called shortsighted; 2025-02 risk a small fraction of closed core capital; 2025-08 static ATR-normalised bets; 2025-10 closed-balance sizing; 2026-03 fixed vol targeting understates tails; 2026-05 says ATR/variance is the control; 2026-07 absolute leverage cap and equal risk. Reasons given: convexity, path dependence and Kelly noise, not new data. (3) Number of systems: about 20 (2024-10) to depends-on-regime (2024-12) to about 10 saturation (2025-08), reason not explained. (4) Regime outlook: Oct 2024 correlated reversals and chop, mid-2025 deep drawdown, then 'trend heaven' (2025-10) and best in years (2026-01), reason given is central-bank decoupling and fragmentation. (5) Typology: two tribes (2025-06) becomes four species (2025-08). (6) Passive: 2026-05 adds the passive/inelastic-markets argument not present before.

disagreements.topic: How many genuinely different trend systems exist and whether extra models/markets diversify
disagreements.their_position: Runs eight core systems with variations to reach 20; more uncorrelated systems keep improving drawdown and MAR; extra models help in outlier regimes, hurt in calm ones (10 beat 20 without outliers)
disagreements.other_position: Only five to ten ways to do trend following; extra models/markets have diminishing returns and may concentrate on the same theme; 70-80 less correlated markets better than hundreds

disagreements.topic: Breadth: is 100+ markets the edge or a design preference
disagreements.their_position: For an outlier hunter maximum feasible breadth is non-negotiable; random 30-market subsets of 68 beat the full book 12% of the time
disagreements.other_position: No performance evidence that 300-500 markets is better; long-lived managers have similar rolling 10-year returns; some of the best outlier-camp funds trade only 20-40 markets; asks for a saturation number

disagreements.topic: Position sizing: closed balance and static bets versus dynamic (volatility) sizing
disagreements.their_position: Closed-balance realised capital is survivable capital; open equity is illusory; vol targeting clips winners and rests on recent vol predicting the future; outlier hunter holds and pyramids (cocoa 2024)
disagreements.other_position: Neither is right; dynamic sizing used by most managers for 25-30 years; open equity in liquid futures is not illusory; inflows break inception-date logic; vol-scaled followers cut cocoa 80-90% of notional; static bets can balloon; Dunn uses a daily risk target not vol target

disagreements.topic: Definition of risk and usefulness of VaR
disagreements.their_position: Risk is permanent loss/vulnerability, not volatility; Sharpe, std dev, VaR fail because crises come from the unforeseen; VaR is popular because quantifiable and smoothing is marketable
disagreements.other_position: Total permanent loss is rare in any strategy; correlation-aware VaR is a decent measure better than Sharpe; big managers target risk, and small daily adjustments suit large AUM and footprint

disagreements.topic: Asymmetric long/short rules, speed, and short-term trend as crisis hedge
disagreements.their_position: Asymmetry reflects structure and improves tail capture; fast systems get whipsawed out of long trends; short speeds suit only some objectives
disagreements.other_position: Asymmetric rules look like optimisation, identical rules arguably more robust; only crisis-offset goals justify short speeds and in 2025 short-term funds did not deliver crisis alpha

disagreements.topic: Do structured products offset passive's effect; usefulness of Trend Barometer; confidence in multiplier
disagreements.their_position: Structured products damp moves and concentrate leveraged risk, may hurt trend; Barometer is a good leading indicator for his lagging fund; multiplier about 5 (range 3-7) but needs verification
disagreements.other_position: Wonders if structured products partly fill the convergent role; Barometer mainly describes month-end trend environment, not a trading tool; asks if 5 can be proved

disagreements.topic: Do trend followers amplify or dampen spikes; why bigger managers had worst drawdowns; is prediction pointless
disagreements.their_position: Trend followers are divergent amplifiers that help create fat tails; big managers' correlation-conscious design was built for 2008-2020; path prediction is futile but recognising structure is not prediction
disagreements.other_position: With dynamic sizing they sell near the top and may dampen moves; big managers tilt to financial futures and lose commodity diversification; asks whether macro forecasters are making a category error

disagreements.topic: Renaissance external fund and analytically optimal parameters
disagreements.their_position: External fund was forced into medium-long trend models by capacity and did marginally; analytic rules give rigour and quick transfer to new markets but are not a savior
disagreements.other_position: Sceptical of the Medallion story; cannot confirm they used trend following; optimal parameters cannot be a holy grail, edge would vanish if everyone derived them

disagreements.their_position: Young/smaller markets trend and diversify (Kaufman); 2020 monetary regime shift produced outlier trends
disagreements.other_position: Carver: no significant effect, diversification only; Beer: open question, uses it to allocate alpha

disagreements.with: Mark Resiminski; Yov Git; Katie Kaminski; Nick Balters
disagreements.topic: Is return dispersion across CTAs healthy
disagreements.their_position: Healthy, trend following is a broad church, but managers must explain objectives
disagreements.other_position: Resiminski: unhealthy, blurs what a CTA is; Git: dispersion is diversification, real problem is a homogeneous index-like universe; Kaminski: both challenge and positive, needs education; Balters: some good, large triggers aggressive selection

disagreements.with: Yov Git; Katie Kaminski; Andrew Beer
disagreements.their_position: Never obvious; claims of obviousness are hindsight and relying on a precedent regime is overfitting
disagreements.other_position: Git: obviousness comes from investor objective; Kaminski: only consistent with an objective; Beer: very few obvious

disagreements.with: Alan Dunn; Nick Baltas; Katy Kaminski; Rob Carver
disagreements.topic: CTA replication as access to trend returns
disagreements.their_position: Lacks a track record across regimes; replication risk
disagreements.other_position: Dunn: performed reasonably and established; Baltas: matches underlying CTAs, existential risk if managers reverse; Kaminski: one access point; Carver: bottom-up better, cheap exposure matters

disagreements.topic: Long-vol overlays on traditional portfolios; what moves prices; diversification; options versus trend with stops
disagreements.their_position: Long-vol overlay is a band-aid on a poor return stream (but accepts combining trend with options); transactions and about 25% divergent feedback move price, fundamentals/flows downstream; markets permanently coupled, diversification adds right-tail exposure; stops give a synthetic option at implicit cost of whipsaw and gap risk
disagreements.other_position: Overlay frees capital for upside (return stacking); positioning of price-insensitive rule-bound flows is the only thing that matters; diversification beneficial only across bounded-loss unbounded-upside positions; buy long-dated options for guaranteed payoff (limited by efficient vol markets)

disagreements.topic: Why trends exist; whether AI ends them; whether correlated markets add diversification
disagreements.their_position: Trader impact is the root, behaviour and fundamentals are derivative; AI agents exert impact too so trends persist; price-correlated markets (Brent/WTI) can still diversify for an ensemble outlier hunter
disagreements.other_position: Behavioural bias and fundamentals drive trends; AI may make markets efficient enough to end them; choose one of two highly correlated markets

internal_tensions.issue: Resizing for volatility: he says positions are never resized down after entry (cocoa 2024 held and pyramided; static ATR-normalised bets) and that vol targeting is shortsighted, but he also says ATR sizing makes position size shrink automatically when an instrument's variance rises and that variance is the control for cutting and backing off, and he keeps a trailing stop on every system.

Backtests 'cannot predict the future' and are only for sensitivity, yet he reports backtest-derived results as support (68-market 2020-2025 subset test with MAR 0.8 and 88%, 10 versus 20 model test, 40-year trend reshuffles, 125-year Dow/S&P), none shown or validated out of sample.

Number of systems and value of diversification: up to 20 systems that keep improving drawdown and MAR (2024-10) versus 10 versus 20 depending on regime (2024-12) versus saturates at about 10 (2025-08); and markets are fickle in correlation so add systems not markets (2025-06) versus breadth is the edge and new capital goes to markets first (2025-08, 2026-07), yet diversification does not thin tails or cure correlation.

Predictability: markets are 'mostly predictable and regime-based' with regimes observable (a threshold of divergent share), and trend models act as thermometers/regime forecasters, versus the future is unfinished, path prediction is futile and the advantage lies only in response.

Trend structure 'has never weakened' (Hurst never below 0.62, fingerprint survived every era) yet 2010-2018 is 'the anomaly' for trend following, correlation-conscious managers won 2008-2020, and the current regime is claimed the best in years; the structural feature and the opportunity set are not reconciled with a test. Also passive growth is said to raise trend opportunity although the fingerprint threshold was crossed long ago and cannot show it.
Hurst 0.866 is used as proof of memory while daily directional autocorrelation averages near zero; the memory is said to sit in magnitude and clustering, with a second research phase promised.

Correlations: hidden correlations make many trends reverse together (Oct 2024) while outlier moves are said to break cross-market correlations; markets are permanently coupled and in crisis everything correlates (2026) yet diversification across correlated Brent/WTI is claimed to work.

Risk defined as permanent loss with few trend followers blowing up, but he also accepts deep long drawdowns as inherent (April-May 2025, SG Trend Index worst monthly drawdown) and realistic drawdown of 35-40% rather than 5-10%.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A time-series momentum book on about 68-100 diversified futures markets beats random 30-market subsets of itself on MAR roughly 88% of the time, and 27 of 68 markets lose money while the book earns MAR near 0.8; test on longer history and out of sample.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Daily futures for 68+ markets, 1984 onward, back-adjusted; equal-weight ATR-normalised absolute momentum; random subset resampling

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Static entry sizing (equal ATR-normalised risk, no later resizing) beats daily vol-targeted resizing on skew and compound return for a wide trend book, because vol spikes mid-trend clip the largest winners; the reverse holds under a low-vol-budget mandate.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Same book with static versus vol-scaled/risk-target variants; top-trade contribution; per-trade vol-spike events

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Sizing new risk from closed balance rather than open equity reduces drawdown depth and ruin probability for the same expectancy, at modest cost in return.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trade-level P&L with timestamps; simulation of closed-balance versus equity sizing including inflows

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Equal-risk fractional sizing beats Kelly or edge-tilted sizing out of sample across regime changes, because edge differences are smaller than estimation noise.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Per-market rolling edge estimates; compare equal-risk, Kelly and tilted books

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A 20-system ensemble per market beats a 10-system ensemble in outlier (chaotic) regimes and loses to it in outlier-free regimes; system count shows diminishing but non-zero MAR gains until margin binds.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Ensembles of 8 model classes with parameter variations, regime flag for outlier presence

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Return streams of the same trend ensemble applied to highly price-correlated markets (Brent, WTI) are quite uncorrelated, so including both improves diversification.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Brent and WTI futures; ensemble trade returns; correlation of trade-level and monthly returns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Pure absolute momentum outperforms the same signals with a cross-sectional ranking overlay on top-trade capture, but the overlay gives smoother returns and lower correlation.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Same universe with and without cross-sectional ranking; top-trade share, skew, MAR

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Asymmetric exits (looser exits on commodity longs, wider trailing stops on equity shorts) improve tail capture and MAR relative to identical symmetric rules.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Per-asset-class symmetric versus asymmetric exit variants; out-of-sample split

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Medium-to-long trend systems outperform short-term ones, and short-speed trend funds do not provide crisis alpha, over multiple decades.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Lookback-specific trend returns across markets; equity drawdown period returns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Walk-forward (develop 1970-2000, freeze, run 2000-2024) drawdown for a trend system is 35-40% versus 5-10% in the full backtest, and CAGR falls correspondingly.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Multi-market futures 1970-2024; frozen rule set; backtest versus OOS drawdown and CAGR

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A share of divergent participation above roughly 20-30% (proxied by trend/momentum/passive/forced-flow share) flips markets into trending regimes with fat tails and volatility clustering; below it the market ranges.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Proxy for divergent participation (positioning, CTA/passive share, stop-driven flow); per-market Hurst, kurtosis, vol autocorrelation

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Rising price-insensitive ownership (passive share) raises the price impact per dollar of flow and widens overshoots, improving trend following; and the fingerprint (Hurst, kurtosis) is not visibly changed.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Passive share series, flow-to-price impact estimates, rolling Hurst and trend-index returns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Trend-following returns are higher when central-bank policy is decoupled/uncoordinated (and policy-whipsaw low) than in coordinated QE regimes; the 2010-2018 period is the low-performance anomaly.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Policy-rate dispersion/coordination measure, QE periods, trend index returns by era

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Correlation-conscious, cross-sectional vol-targeted trend managers beat idiosyncratic time-series managers in 2008-2020 and underperform after 2020.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Manager-level returns classified by style; post-2020 split

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Prolonged low realised volatility (calm) precedes larger shocks and drawdowns, more so when vol-targeted leverage has built up; options are cheapest then.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Realised vol percentile, subsequent tail events, systematic leverage proxies, implied-vol levels

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A 50/50 mix of S&P 500 and a trend (or long-vol) program yields returns close to the sum rather than the average because correlation turns negative in crises.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: S&P total return and trend index monthly series; crisis-period correlations

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Over 40 years the 10 best S&P months contribute about 30% of growth and the 10 worst months a 40% drag, so protection with open upside raises compounded wealth.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Monthly S&P series, scenario removal of best/worst months

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Rules that use absolute price levels, long-lookback percent returns, mean reversion to long averages or fixed dollar stops give biased signals on Panama back-adjusted futures versus ratio-adjusted or adjustment-agnostic indicators.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Raw contract data, Panama and alternative adjustments, matched live roll logic

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Adding to winners as the trend persists (anti-martingale with a staggered ensemble) gives higher skew and MAR than constant-size entry; martingale doubling yields small gains and catastrophic risk.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Variants with staggered system activation versus single entry; skew, top-trade share

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A Faber-style long-only 10-month moving-average overlay on SPY/TLT/EEM limits large drawdowns but lags re-entry in sharp recoveries and whipsaws in sideways markets.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: SPY, TLT, EEM monthly total returns; SMA10 rule; drawdown and whipsaw count

blind_spots: (reader) Never shows a track record, return, Sharpe/MAR or drawdown series for his own fund; the only own numbers are one-off statements (metals about 21% in 2025, good January 2025, April 2025 worst drawdown) and a back-test-like MAR 0.8 on 68 markets.

(reader) Entry, exit and trailing-stop rules, the stop distance, the list of 8 system classes and the rule for system activation are not specified; the risk fraction per trade is given only as examples ($500, 2% expectancy, 'very small fraction').

(reader) The agent-based model, the 25% threshold and the 68-market fingerprint study are unpublished and unshown; the divergent share in real markets is never measured, and the threshold varies between 20-25%, 25-30% and about 25%.

(reader) No transaction-cost, slippage or capacity analysis for a roughly 100-market book with small illiquid markets (live cattle, rubber, milk), beyond avoiding unregulated venues and a CFD swap discussion in 2024.
(reader) No account of how closed-balance sizing and static bets would have behaved in a test; asserted with worked examples only; no out-of-sample or live comparison against vol targeting.
(reader) Never addresses carry, value, fundamentals or valuation signals as complements (carry appears only as positive swap on CFDs), nor how short positions pay in non-crisis regimes.

(reader) Regime explanations (policy coordination, fragmentation, passive growth) are narrative and ex post; no indicator of coordination or of trend-friendliness is defined or tested, and the same structure is said to be permanent.

(reader) Unsourced statistics: 60% passive, 40-year S&P best/worst months, 5,791x five-sigma frequency, 90% endogenous moves, WHO fertility, 50/50 chart; examples are cherry-pickable (cocoa, wheat, gold, oil).
(reader) Heavily dependent on a few events in 2020-2025 (cocoa, wheat, gold, oil) with a sample of 3,264 trades; the long-history claims (1970-2024, 125 years) are asserted without data shown.

(reader) Does not discuss the cost of staying invested in no-outlier regimes in dollar terms for investors (decade-length cocoa wait of about 15 years) or how clients should size an outlier-hunter allocation.
reader_inferences: (reader) Operationally this is a high-skew, low-hit-rate (30-40% winners) absolute-momentum strategy on a very wide universe with static equal-risk entries, ensemble pyramiding and trailing stops; it should be evaluated on skew, top-trade share and MAR over long samples, not on Sharpe or short-term rankings, and compared with SG Trend and vol-targeted peers.

(reader) His two main differentiators for testing are (a) breadth beyond about 70 markets with no cross-sectional ranking, and (b) no volatility resizing after entry plus closed-balance sizing; both are testable with public futures data and a trade log.

(reader) The regime claim reduces to testable conditioning variables: central-bank coordination/policy dispersion, QE periods, compression (low realised vol) followed by shocks, and passive share; the hypotheses should be registered before looking at holdout data.

(reader) His distrust of Gaussian tools and his reliance on ruin/survival suggest preferring drawdown, ruin probability and geometric growth with reshuffled paths over Sharpe when comparing his rules with others (e.g., Carver, Kaastrup-Larsen).

(reader) Overlap with Dave Dredge's convexity framework (brakes and acceleration, barbell, options versus stops) is large; claims quoted from Dredge in MT107, MT186, MT222 and MT224 may be adoption of Dredge's ideas rather than independent evidence.

(reader) The role label for the same person varies across the pack (East Coast Capital Management in MT107, Stockcross in MT181, 'at Dunn' in MT222 as the ledger gives it, East Coast/Australia elsewhere); treat firm affiliation as uncertain, and note that several early appearances (MT019, MT063, MT105) lean on speaker attribution by content.

(reader) His rule of thumb that structure (the engine) is permanent but opportunity varies suggests a two-layer model for a strategy: a permanent trend allocation (harvest) and a conditional exposure sized by regime indicators, which he declines to do himself (he stays always on).

(reader) Statements about AI and LLMs (pattern matching, overfit, will not end trends) are consistent across MT019, MT057, MT105, MT181 but are asserted; they matter mainly as a reason he keeps to medium-long horizons.
